messages.author: e5841ce9d01eda50
messages.subject: Error in parboot: invalid size argument
parts:
Hello everyone,
I'm having trouble finding any information about this error in the group or anywhere else, and haven't been able to fix it on my own.
I have created and run my global model in gdistsamp and would now like to run a GOF test with bootstrap iterations to determine model fit.
I ran fitstats, which seems to work fine, but then when I run the bootstrap function I get an error about an "invalid second argument 'size'".
Any thoughts??

> fitstats <- function(g.global) {
+   observed <- getY(g.global@data)
+   expected <- fitted(g.global)
+   resids <- residuals(g.global)
+   sse <- sum(resids^2, na.rm = TRUE)
+   chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected, na.rm = TRUE)
+   freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2, na.rm = TRUE)
+   out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
+   return(out)
+ }

> (g.pb <- parboot(g.global, fitstats, nsim=10, report=5))

t0 = 97959.52 3578.87 2954.002 
Error in rmultinom(1, N, prob = cp.it) : invalid second argument 'size'
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In rnbinom(1, mu = lambda[i], size = alpha) : NAs produced
2: In rbinom(1, Ns, phi[i, t]) : NAs produced

Dear Adrienne,

the cheapest means of dealing with missing covariate values in your situation is to simply replace the missings with the mean of the covariate values measured at the other sites. There are more elegant, and more correct ways of dealing with missing covariates, but they are all much more complicated in a sense, and since you only have a very small proportion of sites with missing covariates, doing this cheap solution will hardly affect anything.

Best regards  --- Marc

I am much more conservative than Marc.  Unless one could justify (to others and not just to yourself) that the reason for missing data was not related to the factors being investigated, I would not plug in the averages or use fancier imputation methods.  If one can justify the use of the imputation methods, that's great.  But not at all just to make software not print errors or warnings.  This is especially true if one might face court challenges if some management decisions were to be based on your analysis.

Jim

Admittedly, I'm a bit cranky in my old age.

If this was for a Master's Thesis or a homework problem, the consequences of any action would likely not be major no matter what was done.  But hopefully one would be able to come to the conclusion that the data was "missing at random" and just toss those sites (because there are so few sites) or perform some simple imputation.

If this was for supporting an upcoming land management decision (or a medical decision for a pharmaceutical company), I would investigate and document the cause for the "missingness."  Depending on the kind of "missingness", I'd make a decision of whether to perform some sort of imputation, drop the offending sites, or not do the analysis at all and treat that as a lesson learned.  (Yes, I know few would feel they have the luxury of not doing the analysis.  But that might be considered more often than not.)  If the analysis is still to be performed and reported, then the missingness and the associated actions need to be well documented and justified and prominently included in the report.

Jim
